title: SpaceX Stock Hits Record Low as Heat Shield Doubts and Lockup Fears Mount
excerpt: Shares closed at $108.37, down 20% from the $135 IPO price six weeks ago, as NASA scientists question Starship's thermal protection system and insider lockup expirations loom.
body:
• SpaceX shares closed at $108.37 on Friday, a record low and 20% below the $135 IPO price set just six weeks earlier, with the market capitalization dropping more than $1 trillion from its June high.
  • NASA scientists called Starship's current thermal protection system a "dead end" for achieving full-and-rapid reusability, raising questions about the rocket's core economic promise.
  • Up to 37% of insider shares subject to a 180-day lockup could begin trading as early as August 6, with the first tranche of up to 911.5 million shares potentially hitting the market.
  • SpaceX's 13th Starship test flight was largely successful—deploying 20 Starlink V3 satellites and collecting heat-shield data—but the Super Heavy booster failed to execute a controlled landing.

A Post-IPO Slide Deepens

SpaceX shares fell to a fresh record low on Friday, closing at $108.37—a 3.4% decline on the session and a full 20% below the company's $135 IPO price from mid-June. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average, by contrast, rose 0.7% and 0.5% respectively on the day.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=MxJME2DG-SE

The stock has now fallen for four consecutive weeks. Since its post-IPO high, SpaceX's market capitalization has shed more than $1 trillion, an extraordinary reversal for a company whose debut was one of the most anticipated in years.

"Based on the data from the recent Starship flight, we assert that the current thermal protection system technologies are a dead-end, and cannot get to full-and-rapid reusability."

— Charles Miller, Dan Rasky, and Charles Camarda, NASA scientists

The Heat Shield Question

At the center of the technical debate are the thousands of small, hexagonal ceramic tiles that protect Starship's upper stage from temperatures exceeding 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit during re-entry. The system draws on technology developed for the Space Shuttle, and it works—but at a cost.

After SpaceX's 13th Starship test flight on July 18, three NASA-affiliated scientists published a LinkedIn post calling the current thermal protection system (TPS) a "dead end" for achieving the rapid turnaround times SpaceX needs. The tiles require inspection and replacement after each flight, potentially grounding a Starship for days or weeks between missions.

That timeline clashes with SpaceX's stated goal of cutting the cost of reaching orbit by more than 90% relative to the already-economical Falcon 9 rocket. Rapid reusability—flying the same vehicle multiple times per week—is foundational to that economics. If each Starship needs extensive maintenance between flights, SpaceX would need to build far more vehicles to meet its target of thousands of launches per year.

Flight 13: Success With an Asterisk

The 13th test flight itself was largely successful. The Starship upper stage deployed 20 Starlink V3 satellites—the first operational payload the rocket has carried—and achieved a soft splashdown in the Indian Ocean. A Raptor engine was reignited in space, and the heat shield collected critical data.

"It gave SpaceX all the heat-shield data we needed and then some," CEO Elon Musk wrote on X afterward.

But the Super Heavy booster, which initially fired all 33 Raptor 3 engines during its boost-back burn, ended the burn early. When it attempted to relight 13 engines for a landing burn, only some ignited, resulting in a hard splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico.

"This was not ready for a landing on the launch pad," Bernstein analyst Douglas Harned wrote in a note to clients, calling the booster landing the flight's one "material issue."

Lockups and Short Sellers Add Pressure

Technical concerns are not the only weight on the stock. SpaceX is approaching its first quarterly earnings report as a public company, scheduled for August 4. More consequentially, up to 37% of insider shares subject to a 180-day lockup schedule could be released for trading beginning August 6, with the first tranche potentially as large as 911.5 million shares.

Short sellers have already taken notice. Approximately 110 million SpaceX shares have been borrowed and sold short, representing about 17% of the shares currently available for trading, according to FactSet.

The company's valuation, at roughly 45 times estimated 2026 sales, leaves little room for execution setbacks. SpaceX reported a net loss of $4.28 billion in the first quarter of 2026.

What It Means for Investors

For the Indian diaspora—among the most active retail investor communities in U.S. markets—SpaceX's post-IPO trajectory offers a case study in the gap between visionary promise and near-term execution. The company's Starlink satellite-internet service, a revenue driver with direct relevance to connectivity in India and other emerging markets, depends on Starship flying reliably at scale to deploy V3 satellites.

KeyBanc analyst Michael Leshock remains bullish, suggesting Flight 13 could lead to a booster catch attempt on the next test—"one of the biggest milestones to achieve full reusability." Musk himself has said SpaceX will attempt the catch on Flight 14 unless data review reveals problems.

The next few weeks will be pivotal: earnings on August 4, lockup expirations starting August 6, and the pace of Starship testing will together determine whether the stock finds a floor or continues its descent.
